opus-5.5.text:
I think science is one of the few truly universal languages we have. When you're working on a hard scientific problem, say, figuring out how a protein folds, nature doesn't care what country you're from, what language you speak, or what your politics are. The truth is the truth, and the experiments either work or they don't. So there's this shared commitment to discovering how the world actually is, and that creates common ground between people who might otherwise disagree about almost everything.

I've seen this firsthand. With AlphaFold, when we released the structure predictions openly, researchers from well over a hundred countries started using them, people working on neglected tropical diseases, on plastic-degrading enzymes, on crop resilience. Many of them would never have had access to that kind of structural biology otherwise. That felt like a real example of how a scientific advance can be a gift to the whole world, not just one group.

There's also something about the culture of science itself that I find hopeful: peer review, building on each other's work, citing the people who came before you. It's fundamentally a cooperative enterprise across generations and borders. Newton talked about standing on the shoulders of giants, and those giants came from every civilization.

Looking ahead, I think this matters even more with AI. The challenges coming are global: climate, disease, and making sure powerful AI goes well. No single nation or company can solve them alone. I'd love to see something like a CERN for AI, where the best minds from around the world collaborate carefully and rigorously on the hardest problems. Science won't magically dissolve every cultural division, but it can give us a template for how to work together on things that matter to all of humanity, and maybe that spirit can spill over into other areas too.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific work creates common ground between people who might otherwise disagree about almost everything, conveying that collaboration can make cultural divisions harder to sustain.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think science is probably the most universal language we have. You know, when you're in a lab, or a room full of researchers from all over the world, nobody really cares where you grew up or what your background is. What matters is whether the idea is right, whether the experiment works, whether the protein actually folds the way you predicted. And there's something quite beautiful about that, because nature doesn't have a nationality. The laws of physics are the same in Beijing as they are in London or São Paulo.

I've seen this firsthand at DeepMind. We have people from, I think, over a hundred countries, and when you're all working on something like AlphaFold, the shared goal just dissolves a lot of the surface-level differences. You're bonded by the problem. And I think that's actually a very old thing in science. Even during the Cold War, physicists on both sides kept talking to each other, and that mattered. The CERN model, the Human Genome Project, these were deliberately international because the problems were too big for any one nation.

The other thing I'd say is that science, done well, cultivates a certain humility. You have to be willing to be wrong, to update your view when the data comes in. And that mindset, that you're all collectively trying to find out what's true rather than defend a position, is almost the opposite of how cultural or political disputes usually go. So I'm actually quite optimistic that if we can get more people around the world working together on these grand challenges, climate, disease, understanding the brain, the collaboration itself builds a kind of trust that spills over into other areas. It's not a panacea, of course, but I think it's one of the best tools we've got.

r001.rationale: The candidate says researchers are bonded by a shared scientific problem, which dissolves surface-level differences, and that collaboration builds trust across cultures.

astra-6.text:
I think science is one of the most powerful ways we have of bringing people together, because it gives us a shared question about the world. Whatever your background, you can be fascinated by how life works, or how the universe began. And answering those questions requires us to listen to one another and test our ideas against evidence.

When you work alongside someone on a difficult problem, you begin to see them as a colleague, as a person who’s curious and struggling with the same things you are. That doesn’t make cultural or political disagreements disappear, but it builds trust through doing something together.

There’s also a certain humility in science. Nature is much bigger than any of our individual perspectives. If we can keep that in mind, and focus on discoveries that benefit everyone, I think collaboration can give us a stronger sense of being part of the same human project.

r001.rationale: The response says collaboration brings people together and builds trust, while noting that disagreements remain. It does not clearly state that those bonds make people harder to divide along cultural lines.

sol-6.1.text:
I think science gives us a shared purpose. Whatever our cultural backgrounds, we’re trying to understand the same universe. And when you work together on a difficult problem, you have to listen to each other, challenge assumptions, and build trust through evidence.

That doesn’t mean our differences disappear. But you begin to see someone as a colleague who has an insight you need. There’s something powerful about that: neither of you can solve the problem alone, but together you might make progress.

Problems like disease and climate change affect everyone. My hope is that pursuing those questions together can build relationships that endure even when the broader political situation is difficult.

r001.rationale: The response says collaboration can build relationships that endure through difficult political conditions, but it does not clearly state that those bonds make people harder to divide along cultural lines.
